text:
Officials in Charlotte, North Carolina, have petitioned a judge to dismiss the wrongful death lawsuit over the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee who was killed by a man on a light rail train in the city in August 2025.
Zarutska’s uncle, Frank Scott Haskell, who was hosting Zarutska and her family in Charlotte, filed the lawsuit against the city and its transit security company, Professional Security Services, claiming that Charlotte failed to take reasonable and available safety measures to prevent her murder.
Haskell alleged in the lawsuit that the city and its security knew there were safety and crime issues related to its public transit, and they “were responsible for protecting lawful passengers from known and foreseeable dangers. Their failures caused the fatal stabbing”.
Zarutska was fatally stabbed from behind while aboard a Charlotte blue line train as she was traveling home from her shift at pizzeria. The attack, which was caught on surveillance cameras, gained international attention. Zarutska’s killing became a flashpoint in a broader public debate over violent crime, mental illness and public transit safety.
She had come to the US after living in a bomb shelter in Ukraine and had hopes of finding safety in the US. Family members described her as determined to build a safer life.
She was stabbed by suspect Decarlos Brown Jr, who was charged with first-degree murder and later deemed incompetent to stand trial. He is now in a federal medical facility to restore his competency.
Charlotte’s motion to dismiss the civil lawsuit “with prejudice” comes after mediation talks failed earlier this month.
“The City recognizes the tragic and devastating death of Iryna Zarutska as the result of an intentional criminal attack by Decarlos Brown Jr,” Charlotte’s lawyers wrote. “The City denies that it ignored passenger safety or that its conduct legally caused that attack.”
Charlotte says it “maintained an extensive security program, contracted for armed and unarmed security and company-police services, and undertook initiatives concerning public safety, security planning, training, and transit operations”.
Brown, a homeless man who once told police he was diagnosed with schizophrenia, according to the Charlotte Observer, wrote in a letter to the criminal court that he has “a body emergency. Someone has full access to my body and they are controlling me wrongfully. And law enforcement refuses to investigate it. And it requires an investigation.”
